title: Bloodchild and Other Stories
author: Butler, Octavia E.
review:
Multiple of these are masterpieces imo. Fantastic set of short stories that do a ton within a short page count.

Deeply rich in themes and subtext that also use sci-fi to its fullest extent to look inward at the human condition, our world around us, and ponder on if it's possible for life to be better and what it means to be human.

Also these are incredibly dark and often bleak that feel like realistic futuristic scenarios. Excited to read more from her, they really resonated with me very well.

highlights.text: Freed by the egg and the sting, she would smile and perhaps say things long held in. But tomorrow, she would remember all this as a humiliation. I did not want to be part of a remembered humiliation. Best just be still and know she loved me under all the duty and pride and pain.
Who knows what we humans have that others might be willing to take in trade for a livable space on a world not our own?
Dad had killed Mom, then skinned her completely. At least that’s how I hope it happened. I mean I hope he killed her first.
If you work hard enough at something that doesn’t matter, you can forget for a while about the things that do.

Two DGD parents—both religious, both as opposed to abortion as they were to suicide. So they had trusted God and the promises of modern medicine and had a child. But how could I look at what had happened to them and trust anything?
Healthy people have all the time in the world for stupid generalizations and short attention spans.
He extended a dark, square hand, and I took it and moved closer to him. He was a dark, square man—my height, half again my weight, and none of it fat. He was so bitter sometimes, he scared me.

Scars didn’t bother me much. Disability didn’t bother me. It was the act of self-mutilation that scared me. It was someone attacking her own arm as though it were a wild animal. It was someone who had torn at himself and been restrained or drugged off and on for so long that he barely had a recognizable human feature left, but he was still trying with what he did have to dig into his own flesh.
“People like us don’t get along well together. You must realize that I don’t like you any more than you like me.”
I began the story feeling little hope or liking for the human species, but by the time I reached the end of it, my hope had come back. It always seems to do that.
Calm them. The subcontractor repeated. And she knew then that it meant, literally, “Change them from disturbed people to calm, willing workers.”
People were not supposed to be punished any longer, but of course they were.

“I got pregnant when I was fifteen and again when I was seventeen. Miscarriages both times, thank God.” “It was … rape?” Rune Johnsen asked. “Of course it was rape! Can you actually believe I’d want to give the Communities another human infant to study?”
I just mean human beings ought to be able to behave better than a bunch of rats.” “Many did. Some did not.”

“It mattered more than I know how to tell you that this time my tormentors were my own people. They were human. They spoke my language. They knew all that I knew about pain and humiliation and fear and despair. They knew what they were doing to me, and yet it never occurred to them not to do it.”
“So what will we be, then?” he demanded. “Whores or house pets?”

“May I ask you a question?” And they were walking together on a broad, level dirt pathway bordered by dark, ghostly silhouettes of trees. Night had fallen, and the darkness beneath the trees was impenetrable. Only the pathway was a ribbon of pale light—starlight and moonlight. There was a full moon, brilliant, yellow-white, and huge. And there was a vast canopy of stars. She had seen the night sky this way only a few times in her life.
That was odd, Martha thought. Well, everything was odd. On impulse, she said, “Would you like a tuna-salad sandwich?” “Yes,” God said. “Thank you.”
